Origen of Alexandria (c. 184-253), one of the most brilliant minds in the early church, taught apokatastasis — the final restoration of all things, including the eventual salvation of the devil. Gregory of Nyssa (c. 335-395), one of the Cappadocian Fathers and a key architect of Trinitarian theology, held a similar view, arguing that evil is by nature finite and will eventually be consumed by the infinite goodness of God. Both Origen and Gregory stood well within the mainstream of their era; the condemnation of Origen's broader theological system at the Fifth Ecumenical Council (553) was directed at other aspects of his thought, and scholars debate whether apokatastasis itself was formally condemned.

In the twentieth century, Karl Barth's theology left the door open to universalism, though Barth refused to state it as a certainty. Barth insisted that God's election in Christ is an election of all humanity — that in Christ, God has said "Yes" to the whole human race. Whether this "Yes" is ultimately irresistible, Barth would not say. He regarded universalism as a hope that must not be foreclosed, but also as a conclusion that must not be presumed, because to presume it would be to place a limit on God's freedom.

David Bentley Hart, in That All Shall Be Saved (2019), offered the most ambitious recent defense of universalism, arguing that eternal conscious torment is not merely unappealing but logically incoherent — that a God who creates beings he knows will suffer eternally cannot be called good in any meaningful sense of the word. Hart's argument is philosophical, exegetical, and patristic, drawing on the Greek Fathers to claim that universalism is not a modern invention but the deepest current in the earliest Christian tradition.

Purgatory: The Catholic Position

The Catholic doctrine of purgatory offers a fourth framework. On this view, those who die in God's grace but are not yet fully purified undergo a process of purification after death before entering the fullness of heaven. Purgatory is not a "second chance" for the damned; it is a completion of the sanctification that was begun in this life but left unfinished at death. The doctrine was formally defined at the Councils of Florence (1439) and Trent (1563), though its roots extend back to the early church's practice of praying for the dead — a practice that implies the dead are in a state where prayers can benefit them.

The logic of purgatory is, in some respects, straightforward. Most people who die in faith are manifestly not saints. They retain habits of sin, disordered loves, and incomplete transformation. If heaven is the full experience of God's presence, and if the unreformed soul is incapable of experiencing that presence fully, then some process of final purification seems necessary. The Catholic tradition locates this process after death. Many Protestant theologians, while rejecting the formal doctrine, have struggled with the same underlying question: how does a partially sanctified person become fit for the full presence of God?

C.S. Lewis, an Anglican, expressed sympathy for something like purgatory in Letters to Malcolm: "Our souls demand Purgatory, don't they? Would it not break the heart if God said to us, 'It is true, my son, that your breath smells and your rags drip with mud and slime, but we are charitable here and no one will upbraid you with these things, nor draw away from you. Enter into the joy'? Should we not reply, 'With submission, sir, and if there is no objection, I'd rather be cleaned first'?"

The Biblical Data

Part of the difficulty in the hell debate is that the biblical data is less uniform than any of the positions typically admits. The key terms themselves are complex. "Sheol" in the Old Testament is the shadowy abode of the dead — all the dead, righteous and wicked alike — and carries no connotation of punishment. It is the grave, the underworld, the place where the dead exist in a diminished state. "Hades" in the New Testament roughly corresponds to Sheol and similarly does not always carry a punitive sense. "Gehenna," the term most often translated as "hell" in Jesus' teaching, refers to the Valley of Hinnom outside Jerusalem — a place associated with child sacrifice in Israel's history and, by the first century, with the burning of refuse. Whether Jesus intended "Gehenna" as a literal description of an afterlife destination or as a vivid metaphor for the consequences of rejecting God's reign is a matter of ongoing scholarly debate.

The "lake of fire" in Revelation 20 is explicitly identified within the text as "the second death" — language that the annihilationist reads as destruction, the traditionalist reads as eternal torment, and the universalist reads as the death of death itself. The parable of the rich man and Lazarus (Luke 16:19-31) is often cited as evidence for conscious torment after death, but parables are notoriously poor vehicles for extracting doctrinal propositions — no one argues from the parable of the prodigal son that heaven literally involves a feast with fattened calves.

Why It Matters

The hell debate is not an abstract theological exercise. How you understand hell shapes how you understand God, and how you understand God shapes everything else. If hell is eternal conscious torment, then God is a being who sustains the existence of the damned for the sole purpose of punishing them forever — a being whose justice requires infinite suffering for finite offenses. If hell is annihilation, then God is a being who respects the finality of human choices, even the choice to reject God's love, but does not perpetuate suffering beyond what justice requires. If hell is ultimately emptied, then God is a being whose love is relentless enough to pursue every soul until every soul is won.

Each view has consequences for evangelism, for pastoral care, for the way Christians treat those outside the faith. A Christianity built on the terror of eternal torment will produce a certain kind of convert — one motivated by fear rather than love, one whose relationship with God is fundamentally coercive. A Christianity built on the hope of universal redemption will produce a different kind of community — one less anxious, perhaps, but also less urgent. The stakes are not merely theological. They are human.

What I will not do is tell you which view is correct. What I will do is insist that you know what the options are — that you understand the tradition is broader, more diverse, and more internally contested than the version of hell you were probably taught. The God behind the doctrine matters more than the doctrine itself. And whatever hell turns out to be, the God revealed in Jesus Christ is a God who went to the cross to keep people out of it. That much, at least, is not in dispute.

chapters.title: What Christians Can Learn From Indigenous Spirituality
chapters.summary: The church that destroyed indigenous traditions in the name of Christ had much to learn from the very people it sought to convert. The wisdom it burned is the wisdom it now desperately needs.
chapters.body:
In the opening chapters of Genesis, God places the first humans in a garden and gives them a task: tend it. The Hebrew word is shamar — to keep, to guard, to watch over. The human relationship to the earth, in the Bible's own framing, is not ownership but stewardship. Not dominion in the sense of domination but care in the sense of guardianship. The earth belongs to God. Humans are its caretakers, charged with preserving what they have been given.

This theology is clear in the text. It is almost entirely absent from the practice of Western Christianity. The Christian West — shaped by the Enlightenment, the Industrial Revolution, and the capitalist logic of extraction and consumption — has treated the earth not as a garden to be tended but as a resource to be exploited. Forests have been clear-cut, rivers poisoned, species driven to extinction, and the climate itself destabilized — all within cultures that claimed the Bible as their foundational text. The disconnect between the theology and the practice is staggering.

Indigenous spiritual traditions, across the globe and across their enormous diversity, have preserved what Western Christianity forgot: that the earth is sacred, that humans are part of the creation rather than above it, that the land has a voice and the creatures have a dignity that human ambition does not override. The church that destroyed these traditions in the name of evangelization silenced the very voices that were saying what the Bible itself says. The irony is painful. The cost is incalculable.

Creation Care: What the West Forgot

Indigenous traditions understand the human relationship to the earth in terms that Western Christianity, for all its theological resources, has largely failed to practice. The Lakota concept of Mitakuye Oyasin — "all my relatives" — expresses a relational understanding of the created order in which humans, animals, plants, rivers, mountains, and the earth itself are bound together in a web of kinship. This is not animism in the crude sense that Western missionaries attributed to it — the worship of natural objects. It is a sophisticated ecological theology that recognizes what the Bible affirms and Western practice denies: that creation is a community, not a commodity.

The Haudenosaunee (Iroquois) Thanksgiving Address — recited at the opening of gatherings — names and thanks every element of the created order: the earth, the waters, the fish, the plants, the trees, the animals, the birds, the winds, the sun, the moon, the stars. It is a liturgy of gratitude that takes twenty minutes to recite because it refuses to take any element of creation for granted. It names each gift individually, acknowledges its contribution to the whole, and expresses the community's dependence on and gratitude for what has been given.

Compare this with the average Christian prayer before a meal — a perfunctory few seconds that names God as the source of blessing but says nothing about the earth that produced the food, the animals that gave their lives, the water that nourished the crops, or the human labor that brought the meal to the table. The Haudenosaunee Thanksgiving Address practices, in concrete liturgical form, the theology of creation care that the Bible teaches but the church has reduced to an abstraction.

Wendell Berry — a Christian farmer, poet, and essayist — has spent a lifetime arguing that the church's failure of creation care is not a peripheral issue but a theological crisis. "The ecological teaching of the Bible is simply inescapable," he writes. "God made the world because He wanted it made. He thinks the world is good, and He loves it. It is His world; He has never relinquished title to it." A theology that treats the earth as disposable, Berry argues, has not understood the God who made it. Indigenous traditions that treat the earth as sacred have understood something that the Christian West, for all its theological sophistication, has not.

Community Over Individualism

Western Christianity, particularly in its Protestant and evangelical forms, has become radically individualized. Salvation is a personal decision. Faith is a private relationship with God. The spiritual life is conceived primarily in individual terms: my quiet time, my prayer life, my relationship with Jesus. The community exists to support the individual's spiritual formation, not the other way around.

Indigenous traditions operate on fundamentally different assumptions. The individual exists within and through the community. Identity is communal before it is personal. Decisions are made collectively. Spiritual practices are communal practices. The self is understood not as an autonomous agent pursuing its own spiritual goals but as a node in a web of relationships — with other humans, with ancestors, with the land, with the spirit world — that constitute the self's identity and meaning.

This communal orientation is not foreign to Christianity. It is, in fact, deeply biblical. The New Testament's dominant metaphor for the church is the body — a single organism composed of interdependent members, none of which can say to the others, "I have no need of you." The early church held all things in common. The Hebrew concept of corporate identity — in which the individual is constituted by the community rather than the community by individuals — runs through the entire Old Testament. The Western turn toward individualism is not a biblical development. It is an Enlightenment development that Christianity absorbed uncritically.

Indigenous traditions can help the church recover what the Enlightenment displaced: the understanding that the spiritual life is inherently communal, that the self is formed in relationship, and that the radical individualism of contemporary Christianity is not a feature of the faith but a distortion of it.

The Sacred in the Ordinary

One of the most significant features of indigenous spiritual traditions is the refusal to separate the sacred from the ordinary. There is no division between the spiritual and the material, the holy and the everyday, the place where God is present and the place where God is not. The entire created order is pervaded with spiritual significance. A meal is a ceremony. A walk is a meditation. The land is not the backdrop for spiritual life. It is the medium of spiritual life.

Christianity, in its Western form, has been deeply shaped by the Greek dualism that separates matter and spirit — a dualism that is foreign to the Hebrew worldview in which Christianity is rooted. The sacred has been confined to sacred spaces (churches), sacred times (Sundays), sacred activities (worship), and sacred personnel (clergy). The ordinary — work, eating, walking, planting, resting — has been relegated to the secular, the non-spiritual, the domain of the merely material.

Indigenous traditions know better. And so, it should be noted, does the Bible. The Psalms find God in the mountains, the seas, the storms, and the stars. The incarnation — God becoming flesh, dwelling among us — is the ultimate refusal of the sacred-secular divide. A God who became a carpenter, ate meals with sinners, touched lepers, and washed feet has declared, in the most definitive way possible, that the ordinary is the dwelling place of the holy.

The recovery of this understanding — the recognition that God is present not only in the sanctuary but in the field, not only in the sermon but in the silence, not only in the church building but in the created order that surrounds and sustains it — is one of the most important gifts indigenous spirituality has to offer the Christian tradition. It is also one of the most faithful, because it recovers what the Bible teaches and the church has lost.

The Damage Done in Christ's Name

Any honest engagement between Christianity and indigenous spirituality must begin with an acknowledgment of the damage the church has done. The destruction of indigenous spiritual traditions was not an unfortunate side effect of well-intentioned mission work. It was a deliberate strategy, theologically justified and institutionally implemented. Missionaries and colonial administrators classified indigenous spiritual practices as paganism, devil worship, or superstition — and then systematically destroyed them. Ceremonies were banned. Sacred sites were desecrated. Spiritual leaders were imprisoned or killed. Children were removed from their families and placed in institutions designed to erase their cultural and spiritual identity.

The theological justification for this destruction rested on assumptions that the church must now name and repudiate. The assumption that God was entirely absent from indigenous traditions before the missionaries arrived. The assumption that indigenous spiritual practices were uniformly demonic. The assumption that cultural destruction was a necessary precondition for spiritual salvation. These assumptions are not merely wrong. They are blasphemous — attributing to God the absence of the very creative and sustaining work that Scripture says God performs among all peoples and in all creation.

Richard Twiss and Indigenous Christian Theology

Richard Twiss spent his life demonstrating that it was possible to be both fully indigenous and fully Christian — that the forced choice between the two was a colonial imposition, not a theological necessity. A member of the Rosebud Sioux tribe and an ordained minister, Twiss advocated for indigenous expressions of Christian worship that drew on native cultural forms — drumming, dance, regalia, ceremony — as legitimate vehicles for encountering the Christian God.

Twiss's work was controversial within both indigenous and Christian communities. Some indigenous people viewed him as a collaborator with the religion that had destroyed their ancestors' traditions. Some Christians viewed his incorporation of indigenous cultural forms as syncretism — the blending of Christianity with paganism. Twiss rejected both critiques. He argued that the gospel has always been translated into cultural forms — from the Greek philosophy of the early councils to the Gothic architecture of medieval Europe to the contemporary worship music of American evangelicalism — and that indigenous cultural forms deserve the same dignity and recognition as any other.

"Why is it," Twiss asked, "that an Italian painting of Jesus is considered sacred art, but a Lakota painting of Jesus is considered syncretism?" The question exposes the colonial double standard at the heart of Western Christianity's relationship with indigenous culture. European cultural forms are treated as neutral containers for the gospel. Indigenous cultural forms are treated as contaminated vessels that corrupt whatever they carry. This distinction has no theological basis. It is a cultural prejudice disguised as theological discernment.

Twiss died in 2013, but his legacy continues in the growing movement of indigenous Christian theology — a movement that refuses the colonial binary, claims the gospel on indigenous terms, and insists that the God who created all peoples created their cultures too. This movement is not a threat to Christianity. It is one of its most promising frontiers — a demonstration that the gospel is genuinely universal precisely because it is translatable into every particular culture, including the ones the church once tried to destroy.

The church that learns from indigenous spirituality is not departing from its own tradition. It is recovering dimensions of that tradition that the Enlightenment, colonialism, and Western cultural arrogance have obscured. The God of the Bible is a God of creation, of community, of the sacred in the ordinary. Indigenous traditions have preserved these truths. The church should receive them with the humility of a student, not the condescension of a teacher — and with the repentance of a community that once tried to silence the very voices that were saying what its own Scriptures have always said.

chapters.title: What Evangelicalism Was Supposed to Be
chapters.summary: Evangelicalism was born as a reform movement, an attempt to rescue Protestant Christianity from both the anti-intellectualism of fundamentalism and the theological drift of liberalism. That it became something else entirely is one of the great tragedies of modern American religion.
chapters.body:
The word "evangelical" comes from the Greek euangelion, meaning "good news" or "gospel." In its oldest usage, it simply described anyone who took the gospel message seriously. Martin Luther used the term to describe churches shaped by the Reformation. In much of Europe, "evangelical" remains a synonym for "Protestant." The word carries no political connotation in Germany, Brazil, or South Korea. It is only in the United States that "evangelical" has come to mean something that would be unrecognizable to its founders.

The story of how that happened is a story about good intentions, institutional ambition, cultural anxiety, and the seductive power of political access. It is also a cautionary tale about what happens when a theological identity becomes a tribal one.

The Four Marks: The Bebbington Quadrilateral

The historian David Bebbington, in his landmark 1989 study Evangelicalism in Modern Britain, identified four defining characteristics of evangelical Christianity. These have become the standard scholarly framework, known as the Bebbington Quadrilateral.

The first is conversionism: the belief that lives need to be changed through a conscious, personal encounter with Jesus Christ. This is not merely intellectual assent to doctrines but a transformative experience, what evangelicals have historically called being "born again." The second is activism: the conviction that the gospel must be expressed in effort, particularly in evangelism and social reform. Faith is not private contemplation but public witness. The third is biblicism: a particular regard for the Bible as the ultimate authority in matters of faith and practice. The fourth is crucicentrism: a focus on the atoning work of Christ on the cross as the center of the gospel message.

Notice what is absent from this list. There is no mention of a political party. No reference to a position on immigration, gun rights, or tax policy. No cultural aesthetic. No racial or national identity. The Bebbington Quadrilateral describes a theological orientation, not a voting bloc. That distinction would prove impossible to maintain.

Carl Henry and the Uneasy Conscience

Modern American evangelicalism was born in deliberate reaction against fundamentalism. The fundamentalist movement of the early twentieth century had successfully defended several core Christian doctrines against liberal theology, including the virgin birth, the bodily resurrection, and the authority of Scripture. But it had done so at enormous cost. By the 1940s, fundamentalism had become intellectually isolationist, culturally separatist, and often belligerently anti-modern. Fundamentalist institutions discouraged engagement with secular universities, mainstream media, and the broader culture. The faith was defended by withdrawal.

Carl F. H. Henry, a young theologian and journalist, saw this as a betrayal of the gospel's own logic. In 1947, he published The Uneasy Conscience of Modern Fundamentalism, a slim but explosive book that argued fundamentalism had abandoned the social implications of the gospel. Henry contended that evangelical Christianity had a responsibility not only to save souls but to address the great social evils of the day: racism, poverty, injustice. A gospel that had nothing to say about the world God loved was, Henry argued, an incomplete gospel.

Henry's book was not a call to political liberalism. It was a call to intellectual and social seriousness rooted in orthodox theology. He wanted evangelicals to engage the culture without capitulating to it, to be in the world but not of it, to bring the full resources of Christian thought to bear on public life. This was the founding vision. It was ambitious, noble, and extraordinarily difficult to sustain.

Billy Graham and the Institutional Project

If Henry provided the intellectual framework, Billy Graham provided the charisma and organizational genius. Graham's crusades, beginning in the late 1940s, drew enormous crowds and brought evangelical Christianity into the American mainstream. Graham was handsome, articulate, and media-savvy. He preached a simple gospel message, conversion through faith in Christ, with emotional power and theatrical staging that made him a cultural phenomenon.

But Graham's significance extended far beyond his preaching. In 1956, he founded Christianity Today, a magazine intended to be the evangelical alternative to the liberal Christian Century. Henry served as its first editor. The magazine was explicitly designed to demonstrate that evangelical Christianity could be intellectually rigorous, culturally engaged, and theologically grounded. For a generation, it largely succeeded.

Graham also helped establish Fuller Theological Seminary in 1947, conceived as a graduate-level institution that would train evangelical scholars capable of competing with their mainline counterparts at Harvard, Yale, and Union. Fuller represented the evangelical aspiration to intellectual respectability without theological compromise. Its early faculty included serious scholars like Edward John Carnell, who argued that evangelical theology could meet the standards of academic philosophy.

The National Association of Evangelicals (NAE), founded in 1942, served as the organizational counterpart to the mainline's National Council of Churches. The NAE brought together denominations and parachurch organizations that shared evangelical convictions but rejected fundamentalist separatism. It represented a "third way" between fundamentalism and liberalism, orthodox in theology but engaged with the modern world.

The Evangelical Academy

The institutional project extended beyond media and organizing. Evangelical scholars in the mid-twentieth century undertook a serious effort to establish academic credibility. George Eldon Ladd at Fuller Seminary produced New Testament scholarship that earned respect in mainstream academic circles. F.F. Bruce at the University of Manchester demonstrated that evangelical conviction and rigorous historical scholarship were not mutually exclusive. The founding of the Evangelical Theological Society in 1949 created a professional guild for scholars committed to the authority of Scripture but willing to engage the full range of critical methods.

This academic project mattered because it represented an attempt to hold together what modern culture had torn apart: intellectual rigor and spiritual conviction, critical inquiry and confessional commitment. The evangelical scholars of the 1950s and 1960s believed, with some justification, that liberal theology had sacrificed too much in its accommodation to the Enlightenment, but that fundamentalism had sacrificed too much in its refusal to engage with it. They sought a third way, and for a time, they found it. The tragedy is that the movement's institutional center of gravity would shift away from the academy and toward the television studio, the political action committee, and the megachurch platform.

Francis Schaeffer and the Turn Toward Culture War

The pivot came in the 1970s, and one figure looms large in the transition: Francis Schaeffer. A Presbyterian minister and philosopher who ran a Christian community called L'Abri in Switzerland, Schaeffer had spent decades arguing that Western civilization was in decline because it had abandoned its Christian foundations. His books, including The God Who Is There (1968) and How Should We Then Live? (1976), traced a narrative of cultural decline from the Enlightenment through modern art, philosophy, and theology.

Schaeffer's analysis was often more sweeping than careful, painting with a broad brush across complex intellectual history. But his 1979 collaboration with the future surgeon general C. Everett Koop on the film and book series Whatever Happened to the Human Race? marked a decisive turning point. The project focused on abortion, infanticide, and euthanasia, framing them as symptoms of a civilization that had lost its Christian moorings. Schaeffer argued that evangelical Christians had a moral obligation not merely to preach the gospel but to engage in direct political action to defend the sanctity of life.

This was a fateful shift. Henry had called for social engagement rooted in a comprehensive theological vision. Schaeffer called for political mobilization around specific moral issues. The difference is subtle but significant. Henry envisioned evangelicals as thoughtful participants in the full range of public life. Schaeffer's legacy, whatever his intentions, was a movement increasingly defined by opposition to specific cultural developments: abortion, secularism, sexual liberation, and later, same-sex marriage.

The Moral Majority and Political Capture

Jerry Falwell Sr. founded the Moral Majority in 1979, the same year Schaeffer's anti-abortion work was gaining traction. The timing was not coincidental. Republican strategist Paul Weyrich and others had recognized that evangelical Christians, historically reluctant to engage in partisan politics, represented an enormous untapped voting bloc. The key was finding issues that could mobilize them.

Contrary to popular memory, the initial catalyst was not abortion but the defense of racially segregated Christian schools. The IRS's decision in 1971 to revoke the tax-exempt status of Bob Jones University for its racial policies galvanized conservative Christians who saw it as government overreach into religious institutions. Abortion was grafted onto this mobilization later, largely through Schaeffer's influence. The Southern Baptist Convention, the largest evangelical denomination, had actually passed a resolution in 1971 supporting the legalization of abortion in certain circumstances. It was only in the late 1970s that abortion became the defining evangelical political issue.

The Moral Majority and its successors, the Christian Coalition led by Ralph Reed, the Family Research Council, Focus on the Family, effectively fused evangelical identity with Republican Party politics. This fusion was spectacularly successful in electoral terms. Evangelical voters became the most reliable Republican constituency. But the cost was enormous. Evangelical Christianity became, in the public imagination, a political movement rather than a theological tradition. The Bebbington Quadrilateral was replaced by a voter guide.

The Scandal of the Evangelical Mind

In 1994, the historian Mark Noll, himself an evangelical scholar of impeccable credentials, published The Scandal of the Evangelical Mind. The book's famous opening line was devastating: "The scandal of the evangelical mind is that there is not much of an evangelical mind." Noll argued that evangelicalism had systematically failed to develop a serious intellectual tradition. It had produced gifted preachers and effective organizers but few scholars, artists, or public intellectuals of the first rank.

Noll traced this failure to several sources: the populist anti-intellectualism of revivalism, the dispensationalist theology that devalued engagement with the present world, and the pragmatism that valued what "worked" over what was true. The result was a movement that was theologically shallow, culturally reactive, and intellectually incurious, exactly the opposite of what Henry and Graham had envisioned.

The irony was piercing. The movement that had been founded to rescue conservative Christianity from fundamentalist anti-intellectualism had reproduced that anti-intellectualism in a new form. It had megachurches instead of storefront churches, bestselling books instead of mimeographed tracts, television networks instead of radio stations. But the intellectual depth that Henry had called for remained conspicuously absent.

The Trump Era and the Identity Crisis

The 2016 presidential election brought the contradictions of American evangelicalism into the open with a force that surprised even close observers. Eighty-one percent of white evangelicals voted for Donald Trump, a thrice-married casino mogul who could not name a favorite Bible verse and whose personal conduct violated every standard that evangelical leaders had championed for decades. The leaders who had insisted that "character counts" during the Clinton impeachment suddenly discovered that character was secondary to Supreme Court appointments.

This was not hypocrisy in the simple sense. It was something more revealing. It exposed the degree to which "evangelical" had become a cultural and political identity rather than a theological one. Researchers found that many people who identified as "evangelical" in surveys rarely attended church and could not articulate basic Christian doctrines. They were using "evangelical" as a marker of white, conservative, rural or suburban cultural identity, not a description of their relationship to the euangelion.

The aftermath was a fracture. Prominent evangelical leaders like Russell Moore, then head of the Southern Baptist Convention's Ethics and Religious Liberty Commission, criticized the uncritical embrace of Trump and faced fierce backlash from within the denomination. Younger evangelicals, particularly those of color, began abandoning the label in droves. The historian Thomas Kidd published Who Is an Evangelical? (2019), attempting to recover the historical meaning of the term. Multiple evangelical leaders and scholars publicly renounced the label, not because they had changed their theology but because the word no longer meant what they meant by it.

The Megachurch and the Market

Running parallel to the political capture of evangelicalism was a transformation in its institutional form. The megachurch movement, which exploded in the 1980s and 1990s, represented the marriage of evangelical theology (or at least evangelical aesthetics) with consumer capitalism. Churches like Willow Creek Community Church, founded by Bill Hybels in 1975, and Saddleback Church, founded by Rick Warren in 1980, pioneered the "seeker-sensitive" model: remove the barriers that make unchurched people uncomfortable (hymnals, liturgy, religious symbolism, guilt), and offer a product that meets felt needs (practical sermons, professional music, convenient parking, excellent childcare).

The megachurch model worked spectacularly in numerical terms. By the early 2000s, there were over 1,200 megachurches (defined as congregations with weekly attendance exceeding 2,000) in the United States, the vast majority evangelical or charismatic. But the model also accelerated the transformation of evangelicalism from a theological tradition into a consumer experience. When the church is designed around the preferences of the religious consumer, the consumer's preferences inevitably shape the theology. The hard edges of the gospel, repentance, sacrifice, the cost of discipleship, were sanded down in favor of messages about personal fulfillment, relational health, and financial success. Joel Osteen, whose Lakewood Church in Houston draws over 40,000 weekly, represents the logical endpoint of this trajectory: Christianity as therapeutic optimism, with the cross barely visible behind the smile.

Who Still Claims the Label?

The evangelical world has splintered into at least three identifiable groups. The first is the political-cultural bloc: predominantly white, Republican-aligned, and increasingly defined by opposition to progressive cultural change rather than by theological conviction. This group is numerically dominant and controls most of the movement's institutional infrastructure. The second is the "post-evangelical" contingent: people formed in evangelical churches who retain some evangelical convictions but reject the political and cultural captivity of the movement. Many have migrated to mainline, Anglican, or Catholic traditions, or to independent churches that avoid the evangelical label. The third is the global evangelical movement: churches in Africa, Latin America, and Asia that hold evangelical theological convictions but have no connection to American partisan politics and are often baffled by the American conflation of gospel and party.

What Was Lost

What was lost when evangelicalism became a political identity is precisely what Carl Henry fought to build: a theologically serious, culturally engaged, intellectually honest Christian witness that was beholden to no party and captive to no ideology. Henry wanted evangelicals to bring the gospel to bear on public life. What happened instead is that public life consumed the gospel. The euangelion became a brand. The good news became a platform. And a movement that began as a call to conscience ended as a call to vote.

The recovery of what evangelicalism was supposed to be would require something that movements are rarely capable of: institutional humility, theological self-examination, and the willingness to lose cultural power for the sake of spiritual integrity. Whether that recovery is possible, or whether "evangelical" is now permanently a political word with a thin theological veneer, may be the most consequential question in American Christianity today.

Henry's Uneasy Conscience was prophetic in ways he could not have imagined. The conscience he tried to awaken has been anesthetized by power. Whether it can be revived depends not on elections or institutions but on whether enough people still believe that the good news is more important than the news cycle.

chapters.title: What Happened to the Historical Jesus
chapters.summary: The quest for the historical Jesus has occupied scholars for over two centuries. What they have found — and what they cannot find — matters for everyone who takes the question of Jesus seriously.
chapters.body:
The question of the historical Jesus is not a question about whether Jesus existed. Virtually no serious historian doubts that a Jewish teacher named Jesus of Nazareth lived in first-century Palestine, was baptized by John the Baptist, gathered followers, and was crucified under Pontius Pilate. These facts are attested not only by the New Testament but by external sources — Josephus, Tacitus, Pliny the Younger — and they are accepted by scholars across the theological spectrum, from devout believers to committed atheists. The question of the historical Jesus is a different and more difficult question: What can we know about Jesus through the methods of historical inquiry alone, and what is the relationship between the Jesus of history and the Christ of faith?

This question has occupied some of the finest minds in Western scholarship for over two centuries. The answers have been varied, contentious, and consequential. They have reshaped theology, challenged the church, and illuminated the Gospels in ways that both believers and skeptics ignore at their peril.

The First Quest: Reimarus to Schweitzer

The quest for the historical Jesus began in the eighteenth century with Hermann Samuel Reimarus, a professor of Oriental languages in Hamburg, who argued that the real Jesus was a failed Jewish revolutionary whose disciples, unable to accept his death, invented the resurrection and the entire theological framework of Christianity. Reimarus's work was published posthumously by Gotthold Ephraim Lessing between 1774 and 1778, and it ignited a firestorm that has never fully subsided.

What followed was the first quest for the historical Jesus — a movement, primarily among German liberal Protestants, that sought to strip away the theological layers added by the early church and recover the "real" Jesus beneath. The assumption was that the real Jesus was a simple moral teacher whose message had been distorted by Paul and the early church into a supernatural religion of incarnation, atonement, and resurrection. The questers produced a series of "lives of Jesus" that, with remarkable consistency, discovered a Jesus who looked remarkably like a nineteenth-century liberal Protestant — rational, ethical, undogmatic, and thoroughly modern.

Albert Schweitzer demolished this enterprise in his landmark work The Quest of the Historical Jesus (1906). Schweitzer demonstrated that the liberal lives of Jesus were exercises in projection — each scholar found in Jesus a reflection of his own ideals. But Schweitzer's own proposal was equally radical: the real Jesus, Schweitzer argued, was a Jewish apocalypticist who believed the kingdom of God was about to arrive in a dramatic, world-ending event. When the end did not come, Jesus threw himself on "the wheel of history" by going to his death, hoping to force God's hand. The kingdom did not come, and Jesus died in despair. Schweitzer's Jesus was not a comfortable figure. He was a stranger — alien, mistaken, and ultimately tragic.

Schweitzer's work effectively ended the first quest. The conclusion was sobering: the attempt to find the historical Jesus behind the Gospels had produced not the historical Jesus but a series of mirrors reflecting the assumptions of the questers.

The New Quest and the Third Quest

After a period of scholarly retreat — Rudolf Bultmann and the form critics argued that the Gospels tell us almost nothing about the historical Jesus and everything about the faith of the early church — a "new quest" was launched in 1953 by Ernst Kasemann, one of Bultmann's own students. Kasemann argued that a complete disconnection between the Jesus of history and the Christ of faith was theologically intolerable: if the church's proclamation about Jesus had no grounding in the actual person and teaching of Jesus, Christianity was built on a fiction.

The new quest developed criteria of historicity — tools for identifying material in the Gospels that likely goes back to the historical Jesus. The criterion of dissimilarity holds that a saying or action attributed to Jesus is more likely original if it is dissimilar to both the Judaism of Jesus' day and the theology of the early church (the reasoning being that the church would not have invented material that served neither its Jewish roots nor its own interests). The criterion of multiple attestation holds that material attested in multiple independent sources is more likely historical. The criterion of embarrassment holds that material that would have been embarrassing to the early church — Jesus' baptism by John (implying Jesus' subordination), his cry of dereliction on the cross, his association with sinners and tax collectors — is more likely traceable to Jesus himself, because the church would not have invented it.

The "third quest," emerging in the 1980s and 1990s, shifted the focus from these atomistic criteria to the larger question of Jesus' place within first-century Judaism. Scholars like E.P. Sanders, N.T. Wright, James D.G. Dunn, and John P. Meier argued that Jesus must be understood as a Jew operating within the social, political, and religious world of Second Temple Judaism. The third quest took the Jewish context seriously, studied the historical evidence with rigor, and produced a range of portraits that, while differing in emphasis, converged on several key points.

What Virtually All Historians Agree On

E.P. Sanders, in his influential work Jesus and Judaism (1985), identified a set of facts about Jesus that are accepted by virtually all historians, regardless of their theological commitments. These "almost indisputable facts" include: Jesus was baptized by John the Baptist. He was a Galilean who preached and healed. He called disciples and spoke of there being twelve. He confined his activity to Israel. He engaged in a controversy about the temple. He was crucified outside Jerusalem by the Roman authorities. His disciples continued as an identifiable movement after his death. Some Jews persecuted parts of the new movement.

To these, most historians would add: Jesus taught primarily in parables and aphorisms. He proclaimed the kingdom of God as central to his message. He associated with people on the margins of Jewish society — sinners, tax collectors, the poor. He was known as a healer and exorcist (whether one attributes these to supernatural power, psychosomatic healing, or legend, the reputation itself is historically certain). He clashed with some of the religious authorities of his day, particularly over matters of purity, Sabbath observance, and the temple.

These facts are established on the same grounds as other facts of ancient history — multiple attestation, contextual plausibility, and the presence of material that the early church would have been unlikely to invent. They are not articles of faith. They are conclusions of historical inquiry, accepted by scholars who disagree about virtually everything else.

The Resurrection: What Can History Say?

The resurrection of Jesus is the point at which the historical method reaches its limit — not because the evidence is lacking but because the event, if it occurred, transcends the categories that historical method is equipped to handle.

The historical data surrounding the resurrection are well-established. Almost all scholars — including skeptics like Bart Ehrman and Gerd Ludemann — accept the following: Jesus was crucified and buried. His tomb was found empty shortly after his death (the empty tomb is disputed by some scholars, but the majority position, including among non-Christian historians, is that the tomb was indeed empty). The disciples had experiences they interpreted as encounters with the risen Jesus. These experiences transformed them from a demoralized group of fugitives into a movement willing to die for the proclamation that Jesus had been raised from the dead. The church emerged in Jerusalem, the very city where Jesus had been publicly executed, within weeks of his death — a fact that is difficult to explain if the body was still in the tomb.

N.T. Wright, in his massive The Resurrection of the Son of God (2003), argued that the bodily resurrection of Jesus is the best historical explanation for the convergence of these data. Wright's case rests on two central claims: first, that the early Christian belief in resurrection was a radical mutation within Jewish resurrection belief — the Jews expected a general resurrection at the end of history, not the resurrection of a single individual in the middle of history — and that this mutation requires an adequate cause; second, that no alternative explanation (hallucination, legend, cognitive dissonance) adequately accounts for the empty tomb, the post-mortem appearances, and the explosive emergence of the church.

Bart Ehrman, in contrast, argues that the historian cannot invoke the supernatural as an explanation. "The historian has no access to miracles," Ehrman writes. Historical method, by definition, deals in probabilities, and the probability of any naturalistic explanation — however implausible — is always higher than the probability of a miracle. This is not an empirical finding but a methodological assumption: the historian, qua historian, cannot say "God raised Jesus from the dead," because that claim lies outside the scope of historical method.

The honest assessment is that history can establish that something extraordinary happened — that the disciples were genuinely convinced they had encountered the risen Jesus, that this conviction transformed their lives and launched a movement, and that the alternative explanations all have significant weaknesses. Whether that "something" was a bodily resurrection, a series of visionary experiences, or something else entirely is a question that history alone cannot answer. It is a question that requires a judgment — a judgment informed by history but not determined by it.

Jesus in Scholarly Debate

The third quest has produced multiple portraits of Jesus, each emphasizing different aspects of the evidence. Sanders emphasized Jesus as an eschatological prophet who expected the imminent restoration of Israel. Marcus Borg presented Jesus as a Spirit-filled sage and social prophet. John Dominic Crossan depicted Jesus as a Mediterranean Jewish peasant whose program was one of radical social egalitarianism. N.T. Wright portrayed Jesus as the one who believed himself to be the embodiment of Israel's God, returning to Zion to establish his kingdom. Dale Allison has recently argued that Jesus was a Jewish apocalypticist who genuinely expected the end of the world — and was wrong about its timing.

These portraits are not all equally persuasive, but their diversity illustrates an important point: the historical evidence is rich enough to sustain multiple interpretations. The Jesus of history is not a figure who can be reduced to a single category. He was a teacher, but his teaching was bound up with claims about the kingdom of God that were more than ethical instruction. He was a healer, but his healings were signs of the kingdom, not merely acts of compassion. He was a prophet, but he spoke and acted as one with an authority that exceeded the prophetic tradition. He was a Jew, rooted in the Scripture and traditions of Israel, but he related to that tradition with a freedom that scandalized some of his contemporaries.

Why the Historical Jesus Matters

The historical Jesus matters for faith because Christianity is a historical religion. It makes claims not about timeless truths but about events that happened in space and time — claims that can be investigated, tested, and debated. If Jesus was not a real person who really lived, really taught, and really died, then Christianity is a fiction. If the resurrection did not happen — if the body is still in the ground — then, as Paul wrote, "our preaching is in vain and your faith is in vain" (1 Corinthians 15:14). Christianity stakes everything on the claim that something happened, and historical inquiry is one of the tools we have for evaluating that claim.

But the historical Jesus is not enough by himself. History can establish that Jesus existed, that he taught and healed, that he was crucified, and that his followers were convinced he had been raised. History cannot establish that he was the incarnate Son of God, that his death was an atoning sacrifice, or that his resurrection was the firstfruits of the new creation. These are theological claims that go beyond what historical method can adjudicate. They require a response — not just an assessment of evidence but a decision about what the evidence means, a willingness to trust, a readiness to follow.

The historical Jesus matters because he keeps the church honest. He prevents Christianity from becoming a purely spiritual religion disconnected from the real world — a religion of ideas without a body, of doctrines without a life. The Jesus who sweated in the Galilean sun, who ate with sinners, who wept at a friend's tomb, who overturned tables in the temple, who cried out in anguish on the cross — that Jesus is not a theological abstraction. He is a person. And the Christian claim is not merely that he existed but that he is alive, and that everything depends on what you do with him.

That is not a historical conclusion. It is an invitation. History brings you to the threshold. What you do at the threshold is between you and the one who stands on the other side of it.

chapters.title: What the Gospel Actually Is
chapters.summary: The gospel is not advice about how to be good or how to feel loved. It is news about something God has done. And news is more demanding than advice.
chapters.body:
A man stops you on the street and tells you the war is over. He does not tell you to end the war. He does not give you seven steps for ending wars, or assure you that deep down the war was already over inside your heart. He tells you a thing that happened. The guns are silent. The enemy has surrendered. Go home.

That is what the word gospel means, and we have nearly lost it. Euangelion, the Greek word the New Testament uses, was not a religious word when the church took it. It was a word from the herald and the battlefield, the announcement of a victory or the birth of an emperor. An inscription carved in the marketplace of Priene around the year 9 before Christ called the birthday of Caesar Augustus good news, euangelion, for the whole world, the arrival of a savior who would end war and order the earth (Wright 2015). The first Christians knew exactly what they were doing when they took that word. They walked into the empire's own vocabulary and said the real good news, the actual turning point of history, is not the birth of the emperor. It is the death and resurrection of a crucified Galilean. The gospel was a counter-announcement before it was anything else. It was news, and it was treason.

We have turned it back into advice.

Take the strongest version of the first way we do that, because it is the sincere one. The gospel, many good people will tell you, is the call to follow the example of Jesus, to love your neighbor, to live the Sermon on the Mount, to be a decent and compassionate human being. This instinct is guarding something real. It will not let faith collapse into a private feeling that changes nothing about how a person treats the poor or the enemy. It remembers that Jesus said depart from me to people who called him Lord and did nothing. A gospel that produces no life is a corpse, and the moralist is right to refuse it.

But follow the instinct to its end. If the gospel is fundamentally advice about how to live, then it is not news, and it is not good. It is a ladder, and you already know how the ladder ends, because you have been climbing some version of it your whole life and you are tired, and you are not at the top, and the rung you are standing on will not hold your weight much longer. Advice assumes the war can still be won by the listener. The whole problem is that it cannot.

Now the other way, the gentler one. The gospel, a great many will tell you, is simply that God loves you exactly as you are, full stop, no conditions, no demands. This too guards something precious. It refuses to let grace become a transaction, refuses the cruelty of a God you must satisfy before he will have you. It remembers that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us, that the love came first and uninvited. The sociologist Christian Smith, studying what American teenagers actually believe, found that this had become the real religion of the country, a creed he named moralistic therapeutic deism, in which God exists mainly to make people feel good about themselves and to be available when needed (Smith 2005). It is gentle. It is not nothing. It is half of something true.

But severed from the cross, that love becomes mere sentiment, a warmth that asks for nothing and therefore changes nothing and therefore cost nothing. Dietrich Bonhoeffer named it in 1937 and the name has never been bettered. Cheap grace is the grace we bestow on ourselves, the preaching of forgiveness without requiring repentance, grace without the cross, grace without Jesus Christ (Bonhoeffer 1937). A love that cost the lover nothing is not the love the New Testament is talking about. The love the New Testament is talking about has a body and the body has wounds.

Both ways make the gospel something about you, your effort or your worth. Paul refused both. When he set down what he meant by the gospel, in the fifteenth chapter of his first letter to Corinth, he did not give an ethic and he did not give a reassurance. He gave a report. I delivered to you as of first importance what I also received, that Christ died for our sins in accordance with the Scriptures, that he was buried, that he was raised on the third day, and that he appeared, to Peter, to the twelve, to more than five hundred at once, most of whom are still alive (1 Corinthians 15:3-6 ESV). It is a list of events with a list of witnesses, datable, public, the kind of claim that can be checked and therefore the kind of claim that can be false. J. Gresham Machen, watching the faith dissolve into ethical idealism in 1923, put it as plainly as it can be put. Christianity depends, he wrote, not upon a complex of ideas but upon the narration of an event (Machen 1923). From the beginning the gospel was news.

And the news has a center, and the center is the cross, and the cross is doing the work, not decorating the end of it. Christ died for our sins. The little word for is the engine. It means the death was in our place, that the war we could not win was won by someone else taking the loss that was ours to take. You cannot hear this as good news until the bad news has landed, until you have understood that you are not the neutral civilian in this story but the losing side, that the thing the cross addresses is not your low self-esteem but your guilt. The order matters more than almost anything in the Christian life. Grace offered before the law has done its work is cheap, and grace withheld after the law has done its work is cruelty. Tim Keller spent his ministry on one sentence about this. The gospel is neither religion nor irreligion, neither the moralist's ladder nor the libertine's shrug, but a third thing the world keeps failing to imagine, that we are more sinful than we ever dared believe and more loved than we ever dared hope, at the same time, in the same act, on the same cross.

Here is the reversal the comfortable reader never sees coming. This is more demanding than any moral program, not less. The ladder asks only for improvement, a better version of the self you already are. The gospel asks for that self's death. It does not want your behavior tidied. It wants the whole man handed over, the will, the record, the future, exchanged for a life you did not earn and cannot manage and will spend the rest of your days learning to receive. Grace is not the absence of demand. It is the most total demand there is, because it claims everything, and it gives everything, and there is nothing left over that is still yours to control. Cheap grace is easy because it leaves you on the throne. The real thing costs you the throne.

I have preached the advice and called it the gospel. I have stood up on a Sunday and sent people home to try harder, to be kinder, to do better this week, and called that the good news of Jesus Christ, and it was the moralist's sermon wearing a worship band's clothes. I have done it because advice is safe and news is dangerous. Advice keeps me useful, the helpful expert with the steps. News makes me a beggar telling other beggars where the bread is, with nothing to offer but the announcement and no way to improve on it. The pull toward advice is the pull away from the cross, and I feel it every week.

The herald does not ask you to win the war. He tells you it has already been won, somewhere outside the city, on a hill, by someone else, and the telling is either the best thing you have ever heard or an offense, depending entirely on whether you still wanted to fight it yourself. Good news to the soldier who is exhausted and out of ammunition and ready to lay it down. Treason to the one who was sure he was winning. The gospel has always been both, and which one it is to you tells you exactly where you are standing.

### Works Cited

Bonhoeffer, Dietrich. 1937. The Cost of Discipleship. Translated by R. H. Fuller. New York: Macmillan.

Keller, Timothy. 2008. The Reason for God. New York: Dutton.

Machen, J. Gresham. 1923. Christianity and Liberalism. New York: Macmillan.

Smith, Christian, with Melinda Lundquist Denton. 2005. Soul Searching: The Religious and Spiritual Lives of American Teenagers. Oxford: Oxford University Press.

Wright, N. T. 2015. Simply Good News. New York: HarperOne.

chapters.title: Where Do Right and Wrong Even Come From?
chapters.summary: Almost everyone believes some things are really wrong and not just unpopular, and that belief is harder to account for than most people admit.
chapters.body:
Start with something you already believe. Torturing a child for fun is wrong. Not wrong-for-you, not wrong-in-our-culture, not wrong-because-we-voted-on-it. Wrong. If a society passed a law approving it, the law would be evil and the society would be mistaken, and you know this with a confidence that survives every argument anyone has ever made against it.

That conviction is the thing we have to account for. Where does it come from, and what does it tell us about the world?

Let me state the skeptic's case at full strength, because it is a serious case and I held it myself for years. The hardest version goes like this. Human beings are animals shaped by evolution. Creatures that cooperated survived and passed on their genes, so we inherited strong instincts to protect our own, to punish cheaters, to feel disgust at certain acts. What we call morality is the felt residue of those instincts plus thousands of years of cultural negotiation. It feels like we are perceiving a real moral law. We are actually feeling a very deep preference. There is no law out there. There is only the wiring in here, and the wiring is what natural selection found useful.

Notice what this account gets right, because it gets a great deal right. Evolution surely did shape our moral emotions. Cultures do differ on a thousand things. People do dress up self-interest as principle constantly, and a theory that explains how we came to feel moral feelings is doing real work. None of that is in dispute. Francis Collins, who led the mapping of the human genome and was an atheist into adulthood, grants every bit of the biology. He simply noticed that the biology does not reach the thing it was asked to explain.

Here is the gap. An account of how we came to have a belief is not an account of whether the belief is true. Suppose I tell you exactly why you believe two and two make four, tracing it to brain chemistry and childhood and the survival value of counting. I have explained the belief. I have said nothing about whether two and two actually make four. They do, and they would whether or not any creature ever evolved to notice it. The origin story of a belief and the truth of a belief are two different questions, and the evolutionary account answers only the first.

So press the second question. When you say torturing a child for fun is wrong, are you reporting a fact about the act, or are you reporting a fact about your feelings? Everything turns on this. If you are only reporting your feelings, then a person with different feelings is not mistaken, only different, the way someone who dislikes cilantro is not mistaken. But that is not what you mean. You do not mean that you happen to dislike child-torture. You mean it would be wrong even if every human being on earth came to enjoy it. You are making a claim about the act, not about your appetite.

This is the moral argument, and C.S. Lewis put its starting point better than anyone. He noticed that people quarreling do not say I do not like what you did. They say that is not fair, you promised, give me my share. They appeal to a standard they expect the other person to recognize, and the other person almost never replies that there is no such standard. He argues that he did not really break it. Both parties are reaching for a law above them both, the way two men measuring a board reach for a ruler neither of them invented.

The skeptic can answer here, and the answer deserves respect. He can say the standard is real but it is built by us, a contract we make so we can live together, refined over centuries the way law is refined. There is genuine wisdom in this. Much of our actual moral progress does look like negotiation and revision. But the contract account has a hard edge it cannot get past. If right and wrong are only agreements among the powerful, then the reformer who stands against his entire society has no ground to stand on. When abolitionists said slavery was wrong while their whole legal order said it was lawful, they were not proposing a better contract. They were saying the contract itself was evil, measured against something higher than the contract. If morality is only the agreement, the people who broke the agreement to free slaves were simply criminals, and we know they were not. We know they saw something true that their society was blind to. That knowledge requires a standard above every society, the very thing the contract account denies.

It is worth slowing down here, because the contract account is the most respectable secular answer and it keeps coming back in new clothes. Some say morality is what maximizes well-being, the greatest good for the greatest number. Others say it is what a fully rational and impartial person would choose. These are serious proposals and they capture real wisdom about how to weigh competing goods. But every one of them smuggles in a value it cannot justify on its own terms. Why should I care about the greatest good for the greatest number rather than the greatest good for me and mine? Why should I be impartial when partiality so often serves me better? The proposals tell you how to pursue the good once you have already agreed that you ought to. They do not tell you why you ought to, and that ought is the whole mystery. You can build an elaborate machine for calculating the right thing to do and still have said nothing about why the right thing makes a claim on you that you are not free to ignore. The machinery assumes the obligation it was supposed to explain.

There is a sharper way to feel this. Imagine the last truly evil thing you heard about, the headline that made your stomach turn. Now ask what you were actually doing in that moment of revulsion. You were not consulting a contract. You were not running a calculation about social utility. You were perceiving something, the way you perceive that a room is cold or a note is flat, except that what you perceived was a quality of wrongness in the act itself, a wrongness that seemed to be there independent of you, that you discovered rather than invented. That is the raw datum, and any theory of morality has to either explain it or explain it away. The theories that explain it away are tidy. They are also unlivable, because the very people who hold them go on perceiving wrongness as a feature of the world the moment they stop philosophizing and start living.

There is a second pressure point, quieter and harder. Suppose you accept that objective moral facts exist, hanging there in reality the way mathematical facts do. You still have to explain why those facts would have any authority over you. A mathematical fact does not command me. It does not lay an obligation on my will. But moral facts do exactly that. They do not merely describe. They oblige. They say you must, and they hold you guilty when you do not. A bare fact floating in the structure of the universe cannot issue a command, because commands come from persons. The strange and stubborn feature of moral experience is that it feels less like seeing a fact and more like hearing a voice, a summons that is over us and addressed to us. That feature is hard to explain on any view where the universe is, at bottom, impersonal stuff.

This is where the Christian claim earns a hearing. Not because believers are better at being good, they plainly are not, but because the Christian account fits the shape of the experience. If the deepest thing in reality is not stuff but a person, a God whose own character is the standard of good, then moral facts are not free-floating after all. They are grounded in someone, which is why they can command. The voice you seem to hear is a voice. The obligation you feel is owed to someone. The guilt that follows wrongdoing is not a malfunction to be medicated away but an accurate signal that you have wronged not just a neighbor but the One whose image the neighbor bears.

It is worth pausing on why this fit matters, because the skeptic can grant the fit and still shrug. Lots of stories fit the data, he might say, and fitting is cheap. True enough. But notice what the Christian account does not have to do, which is the thing the secular accounts cannot avoid doing. It does not have to pretend that your sense of obligation is an illusion while asking you to keep obeying it. It does not have to call your moral perceptions a useful trick of the genes and then trust those same perceptions to guide your life. It takes the data at face value. There really is a law. It really does oblige you. The guilt you feel when you break it is really tracking something. On the Christian account, every part of the moral experience is exactly what it presents itself as, which is a strong mark in favor of a theory, that it does not have to explain away the very thing it set out to explain.

Be careful here, because Christians overplay this and skeptics rightly call the foul. The argument does not say atheists cannot be good. They obviously can, often better than the religious, and any honest believer has been outclassed in kindness by people who believe nothing. The argument also does not say you need to believe in God to know right from wrong. You do not. A person can read the ruler perfectly while denying that any ruler exists. The claim is narrower and harder to escape. It is that the moral law you already obey, the one you reach for the instant someone wrongs you, makes more sense if it comes from somewhere than if it comes from nowhere. The atheist who lives by it is borrowing furniture from a house he says was never built.

There is one more move worth naming, because it is the most honest one a skeptic can make, and I respect it more than the others. He can simply accept the cost. He can say, with the philosophers who followed this thought to its end, that if there is no God then there really is no objective right and wrong, that our moral convictions are a beautiful and useful illusion, and that we should keep them for the sake of getting along while admitting they point at nothing. This is consistent. It is also nearly impossible to live. The same person who says morality is an illusion will be outraged within the hour at genuine injustice, and the outrage will not feel like a preference. It will feel like a perception of something real. We are built, it seems, to bump into a moral floor that our theories tell us is not there.

So here is where this leaves you, and I am not going to tie it off neatly. You believe, as surely as you believe anything, that some things are truly wrong. That belief is either tracking something real or it is a useful trick your genes are playing. If it is a trick, you will go on living as though it is not, because you cannot do otherwise. And if it is real, then it is the kind of thing that has to come from somewhere, and the somewhere has to be the kind of thing that can issue a command. A law over us, addressed to us, that we did not make and cannot repeal. That has a name. The question is not whether you feel the law. You do. The question is who is speaking.

chapters.title: Why Christianity and Not Something Else?
chapters.summary: The question is not whether Christianity is the only religion with truth in it. The question is whether it makes claims that are unique, claims that matter, and claims that can bear the weight of a life.
chapters.body:
The question comes from honest people, and it deserves an honest answer. In a world of multiple religious traditions — each with its own scriptures, its own saints, its own moral vision, its own account of the human condition — why should anyone prefer Christianity? The question is sharpened by awareness: the person asking it has met Buddhists who are more compassionate than most Christians they know, Muslims whose devotion to prayer puts the average churchgoer to shame, and secular humanists whose moral seriousness exceeds that of many congregations. The claim that Christianity is uniquely true can sound, to such a person, like nothing more than the parochialism of people who have never seriously encountered any alternative.

I want to take the question seriously — not triumphally, not defensively, not with the false confidence of someone who has never felt the force of the objection. I have felt it. I have sat with it. And I have come to a set of convictions that I hold not because I think every other tradition is worthless — I do not — but because I believe Christianity makes claims that are genuinely distinctive, claims that address the deepest human needs in ways that no other tradition addresses them, and claims that I have found to be true in the demanding, unglamorous, daily sense of the word.

What Christianity Shares with Other Traditions

Honesty requires beginning with what Christianity shares with other religious traditions, because the common ground is real and significant. Virtually every major religious tradition affirms the existence of a moral order that transcends human preference. Virtually every tradition teaches that human beings are called to something higher than self-interest — to compassion, to justice, to love, to service. Virtually every tradition provides a community of practice, a rhythm of worship, and a framework for making sense of suffering and death. Virtually every tradition contains genuine wisdom, genuine beauty, and genuine encounters with the sacred.

The Golden Rule appears in some form in nearly every tradition. Confucius taught, "Do not do to others what you would not have them do to you." The Hindu Mahabharata says, "This is the sum of duty: do not do to others what would cause pain if done to you." The Buddhist Dhammapada teaches compassion for all sentient beings. Islam grounds its ethic of justice and mercy in the character of Allah, the Most Compassionate, the Most Merciful. Judaism's Hillel summarized the Torah: "What is hateful to you, do not do to your neighbor. That is the whole Torah; the rest is commentary."

Christians who pretend that these traditions contain nothing of value are not being honest. They are being defensive. And defensiveness is a poor foundation for conviction. The question is not whether other traditions contain truth. It is whether Christianity offers something that the others do not.

What Christianity Claims Uniquely

Christianity makes three claims that are, taken together, unique in the history of human religion. They are not merely distinctive. They are, if true, world-altering.

The first is the incarnation: the claim that the Creator of the universe became a human being. Not that God sent a messenger, or inspired a prophet, or revealed a law — though Christianity affirms all of these. The claim is that God personally entered the human condition: was born, grew, ate, wept, suffered, and died. No other major religious tradition makes this claim. Islam regards the incarnation as blasphemy — the suggestion that God could become human diminishes God's transcendence. Judaism awaits a Messiah but does not expect the Messiah to be God incarnate. Hinduism has the concept of avatar — divine descent — but the avatars are not fully human in the way that Christian theology insists Jesus was fully human. Buddhism has no Creator God to become incarnate. The incarnation is Christianity's most scandalous claim and its most distinctive one.

The second is the resurrection: the claim that Jesus of Nazareth was raised bodily from the dead, and that his resurrection is the firstfruits of a new creation in which death itself is defeated. Other traditions have concepts of life after death. Other traditions teach reincarnation, or the immortality of the soul, or the survival of consciousness beyond physical death. But the Christian claim is not merely that something survives death. It is that death is reversed — that a specific person who was dead is now alive, in a body, and that this reversal is the turning point of all history. The resurrection is not a symbol. It is not a metaphor for spiritual renewal. It is an event — something that either happened or did not — and Christianity stands or falls on whether it happened.

The third is grace: the claim that the human problem — sin, alienation from God, moral failure, death — is solved not by human effort but by divine initiative. Every other major tradition, in one form or another, presents salvation or liberation as something the human being must achieve: through moral obedience (Judaism, Islam), through enlightenment (Buddhism), through liberation from the cycle of karma (Hinduism), through philosophical wisdom (Stoicism). Christianity reverses the direction. Salvation is not something we achieve. It is something we receive. "While we were still sinners, Christ died for us" (Romans 5:8). The initiative is God's. The work is God's. The gift is God's. The human role is not to earn but to trust.

This is what Dietrich Bonhoeffer meant by "costly grace" — grace that is free but not cheap, grace that costs God everything and costs us our self-sufficiency. It is what Martin Luther meant when he described the gospel as an "alien righteousness" — a righteousness that comes from outside us, that is given to us rather than produced by us. It is the most counterintuitive claim in all of religion, and it is the one that, for millions of people across two millennia, has been the most liberating.

The Scandal of Particularity

The deepest objection to Christianity's unique claims is not that they are unverifiable. It is that they are particular. Why one person? Why one time? Why one place? If God wanted to save the world, why not do it in a way that was universally accessible — a truth written in the stars, a revelation given simultaneously to every culture, a law inscribed on every heart without the mediation of a specific historical event?

The scandal of particularity is real, and it should not be minimized. But it should be noted that all significant events are particular. The American Revolution happened once, in one place, to one group of people, and its consequences are universal. The discovery of penicillin happened once, in one laboratory, by one researcher, and it transformed global health. The fact that an event is particular does not make it parochial. It makes it historical. And history, by its nature, is particular.

The Christian claim is not that God is unavailable to those who have never heard of Jesus. The claim is that what God has done in Jesus is the fullest and most decisive revelation of God's character and purposes — and that this revelation, because it happened in history, must be communicated through history: through witness, through community, through the messy, imperfect, often unfaithful process of human beings telling other human beings what they have seen and heard. The particularity of the gospel is not a limitation on God's love. It is a consequence of God's decision to work through history rather than around it.

The Gospel as Public Truth

Lesslie Newbigin, the British missionary and theologian who spent decades in India before returning to a secularized England, argued that the gospel must be understood not as a private religious preference but as public truth — a claim about the way things actually are, a claim that has consequences for all of life, not just the "religious" part of life.

In his landmark work The Gospel in a Pluralist Society (1989), Newbigin observed that Western culture had developed a fatal dichotomy between "facts" (the domain of science, publicly verifiable, universally binding) and "values" (the domain of religion, privately held, not subject to public adjudication). In this framework, religious beliefs are relegated to the category of personal preference — like a taste in music or a choice of diet. You may believe in Jesus the way you believe in the superiority of jazz, but you cannot claim that your belief is true in the same way that the law of gravity is true.

Newbigin argued that this dichotomy is incoherent. The gospel makes claims about history, about the nature of reality, about the human condition — claims that are either true or false, not merely preferred or not preferred. To say "Jesus is Lord" is not to express a private religious sentiment. It is to make a claim about who actually rules the universe. And that claim either corresponds to reality or it does not. If it does, it has implications for politics, economics, education, science, art, and every other domain of human activity. It is not a private matter. It is the most public matter imaginable.
